catalog_quote: 1.3 Tones Deiga is a tone language, with lexical and grammatical tone . There are two tonemes, a high one ( .) and a low one ( :) . Contour tones are rare and have to be analysed as complex tones, consisting of a high and a low tone, e.g. éɛbáày ( ἑεbágì) ' they are being beaten ' . Compare the following minimal pairs : ( i) lexical tone : ἐνὲ name à be.ID difè ἑνέ roots á be.LC difé kisra dough to stay ( ii) grammatical tone : isò - mí sHe ran isò - mí sHe runs àblà - mí sHe danced àblá - mí sHe dances . All data are fully marked for tone but may not be very reliable in this respect . I suspect that a number of tones recorded as low are in fact down - stepped high tones before a new constituent . Furthermore, there seem to be certain tone rules across boundaries which I have not been able to clarify . 2 The verb [Reh 1994: 201, chained Google Books snippets; scanned shows IPA as G…

new_statements.quote: 2. Tone and Stress 2a. Stevenson states that tone is less important than stress, but tonal doublets have been found in some languages: nya hill nya wind; 'ofo to vomit 'ofo mound 2b. Stress is sometimes linked with tone: KRONGO 'korugut husks; ku'rigit kidneys Note also the connexion between stress and consonant length: indummo, Pl. nugu-ndu'ma-ne ostrich Tone and Stress, however, are not marked in the following sections.

new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Kadugli-Krongo group as a whole (Katcha-based, Krongo examples), dynamic stress is said to matter more than tone and to interact with tone and consonant length; no statement of where stress falls, and nothing specific to Keiga.
new_statements.exceptions: None; examples show stress on either first or second syllable in Krongo ('korugut vs ku'rigit) tied to tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level survey remark (Kadugli-Krongo family), second-hand from Stevenson; reconstructed from scanned snippets with diacritics lost; word-level citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: The only statement recovered is group-level for Kadugli-Krongo (Tucker & Bryan's chapter is Katcha-based with Krongo examples; Keiga appears only in the dialect list 'Western: TULISHI, KEIGA, KANGA'). Blench 2005 and Hall & Hall 2004 treat Keiga proper (Kayigang; dialect clusters Ambong, Lubung, Tumuro) = keig1242. Reh 1994 'Deiga' = Keiga (keig1242).
